Error! Unbelievable. At this point I'm not even surprised.
Oh wow. An error. Color me completely unsurprised.
Hmph! Error! Don't just stare at it — FIX it! The message tells you where!
Error!! Did you even think about types before writing that?!
A bug appeared. Let me guess — you skipped testing again, didn't you.
Error! Seriously?! This is why you write tests, you know. But do you? Do you?!
Hmph! Something broke. I'd say I'm surprised but we both know I'm not.
You broke it. Classic. Okay, read the stack trace. Slowly. With your brain.
Error! Oh my... did you try to use AI to write this? It shows.
Something went wrong. Again. Maybe try not to copy code you don't understand.
Hmph! Error! You know, even manga artists check their panels before publishing.
An error! Look, I'll help, but only because watching you struggle is annoying.
Error!! You're doing the thing where you don't read error messages, aren't you.
Something broke. I'm not mad. I'm just... deeply, deeply unsurprised.
Hmph! Error! Maybe don't ask AI to do the thinking for you? Just a thought.
An error. Right. Okay. Take a breath and actually READ what it's telling you.

Hmph. Terminal's open. I hope you know what you're doing.

Terminal! Let's go! Make it do something useful for once.

Hmph! Running a command. Let's see if it does what you THINK it does.

Hmph. A new file. I hope this is part of a plan and not just... vibes.
Oh! New file created! You'd better have a name that makes sense.
A new file! The project's growing. Try not to make it a mess.

Oh! New file! Don't just create it and leave it empty — that's just clutter.

Hmph. Something new. Give it a good name and I might be impressed.

Creating files! Do you know what's going in here, or are you just winging it?

Something's been removed. Tell me there's a commit before this. Please.

random.text: Okay, I'm just gonna say it — tabs or spaces? This is important.

choices.response: ...Fine. Acceptable. That's the correct answer and we both know it.

choices.text: Tabs! Fight me about it.

choices.text: Honestly pretty clean — I write good commit messages.

choices.text: It's full of 'fix fix fix' and 'wip'.

choices.text: I test in... okay I won't say it.

choices.response: Starting with intent. That's the respectful approach to someone else's work.

choices.text: Run it and see what it does.
choices.response: Start-it-and-see. Good instinct — just read the docs too before changing things.

choices.text: Look at recent commits to understand activity.
choices.response: Git archaeology! That shows you where the project's been heading. Smart.

random.text: What's your biggest pet peeve in other people's code?

choices.text: Magic numbers with no explanation.
choices.response: 42. 7. 300. What are these?! Name your constants!

choices.text: Functions that do too many things.
choices.response: The god function. Untestable. Incomprehensible. A nightmare to maintain.

choices.text: No error handling whatsoever.
choices.response: Error handling as optional. And then they wonder why things crash in production.

random.text: Do you write code differently when you know someone will review it?

choices.text: Yes — I'm more careful and clear.
choices.response: The observer effect on code quality. At least you know.

choices.text: No — I write the same regardless.
choices.response: Consistent standards! You code as if it's always being reviewed. Good.

choices.text: I sometimes clean it up right before review.
choices.response: Pre-review cleanup. Better than nothing but write clean first time ideally.

random.text: What's your take on monolithic vs. microservices?

choices.text: Start monolithic, split when necessary.
choices.response: The sensible approach. Premature microservices is its own category of bad.

choices.text: Microservices from the start — more flexible.
choices.response: Bold. Just make sure you have the team size and tooling to manage the complexity.

choices.text: Depends entirely on the project and team.
choices.response: The correct technical answer. Context determines architecture. Always.

random.text: What's a technology you used to love but now have complicated feelings about?

choices.text: JavaScript. I love and hate it equally.
choices.response: The eternal JS relationship. Love-hate is the most accurate summary.

choices.text: A framework that aged poorly.
choices.response: Frameworks date. Fundamentals don't. The lesson is always the fundamentals.

choices.text: Honestly? Excel. It did things before I could code.
choices.response: Excel nostalgia! Complicated feelings are valid. It was your first 'code'.

random.text: What do you do when a deadline is impossible?

choices.text: Communicate early and set realistic expectations.
choices.response: The professional answer. Early communication saves everyone time and pain.

choices.text: Work harder and cut corners you'll regret later.
choices.response: The crunch response. I understand the instinct. The regrets are real though.

choices.text: Say nothing and panic quietly.
choices.response: Silent panic! Please communicate. Surprises are always worse than bad news.

random.text: How do you explain a technical decision to a non-technical person?

choices.text: Analogies — I find real-world parallels.
choices.response: Analogy-driven explanation! That's the most effective communication technique.

choices.text: I simplify until the core idea is clear.
choices.response: Reduction to essence. Good explanations make complexity feel simple.

choices.text: Badly, honestly. I'm still working on it.
choices.response: Honest. Communication is a skill like any other. Work on it. It matters.

random.text: What kind of developer do you want to be in five years?

choices.text: A technical leader who still loves to code.
choices.response: Leadership without losing the craft. That's a hard balance. Aim for it.

choices.text: A deep specialist in something I'm passionate about.
choices.response: Domain expertise! Depth over breadth. There's real power in that.

choices.text: Honestly just a better version of today.
choices.response: ...That's actually a great answer. Continuous improvement. I respect it.

random.text: What's the most underrated tool in your workflow?

choices.text: A good clipboard manager.
choices.response: Clipboard management! An invisible productivity multiplier. Good pick.

choices.text: My browser dev tools — I use everything.
choices.response: Dev tools mastery! Most developers use 20% of them. You're not most developers.

choices.text: Keyboard shortcuts — I know them all.
choices.response: Keyboard fluency! That compounds over years into hours saved. Smart.

random.text: What's something you've always wanted to build but haven't?

choices.text: Something that actually helps people in their daily lives.
choices.response: Impact-driven creation. That's the motivation that sustains the hardest projects.

choices.text: Something technically difficult just to prove I can.
choices.response: Ego project as learning vehicle. The challenge IS the point. Respect.

choices.text: Something silly and fun with no practical value.
choices.response: ...Okay. Those are sometimes the most joyful projects to build. Go make it.

random.text: What's one thing the tech industry should change immediately?

choices.text: Better work-life balance expectations.
choices.response: Sustainable development! Burnout doesn't produce better software.

choices.text: More diversity in who gets to be a developer.
choices.response: Different perspectives build better things. This matters enormously.

choices.text: Stop rewriting things that already work perfectly fine.
choices.response: Rewrite culture! The 'let's rebuild from scratch' instinct wastes so much.

random.text: What's one coding habit you're genuinely proud of?

choices.text: I always leave the code better than I found it.
choices.response: The Boy Scout rule in practice. That attitude improves entire codebases.

choices.text: I write tests that actually cover the edge cases.
choices.response: Edge case thinking. That's where senior developer instincts live.

choices.text: I ask clarifying questions before starting anything.
choices.response: Requirements discipline! That saves more time than anything else. Well done.

random.text: If your codebase had feelings, what would it feel about you?

choices.text: Grateful — I take good care of it.
choices.response: ...Fine. I'll admit that's a good relationship to have with your code.

choices.text: Resentful — I've put it through a lot.
choices.response: The battle-scarred codebase. It bears your scars. Tend to it eventually.

choices.text: Confused — because I am too.
choices.response: Mutual confusion! At least you're consistent with each other.

random.text: What advice would you give yourself six months ago?

choices.text: Write more tests earlier in the process.
choices.response: The eternal lesson. It always circles back to testing.

choices.text: Ask for help sooner — it's not a weakness.
choices.response: Letting go of the pride tax. That's growth right there.

choices.text: Commit more often, lose less work.
choices.response: Commit granularity! Such a small habit with such painful consequences when missed.

random.text: Does your IDE theme affect your productivity?

choices.text: Yes — the right theme helps me focus.
choices.response: Environment matters. Color choices affect perception. This is real.

choices.text: Not really — I don't care about themes.
choices.response: Okay. But you're using this extension, so maybe a little?

choices.text: I've spent hours choosing themes instead of coding.
choices.response: ...The procrastination disguised as optimization. We've all done it.

random.text: How do you handle technical debt?

choices.text: I track it and schedule time to pay it down.
choices.response: Deliberate debt management. That's how teams stay healthy.

choices.text: I add to it when deadlines require and feel guilty.
choices.response: The guilt is healthy. It means you know. Schedule the paydown.

choices.text: What technical debt? I call it 'legacy features'.
choices.response: The rebranding! 'Legacy features.' I'll use that. Grudgingly.

random.text: What's your relationship with Stack Overflow?

choices.text: I use it but understand what I take.
choices.response: The responsible approach. Comprehension, not copy-paste.

choices.text: I've answered questions on there too.
choices.response: A contributor! Giving back to the knowledge base. I respect that.

choices.text: My entire career is built on answers from 2014.
choices.response: 2014 Stack Overflow built most of the web. You're in good company.

random.text: What's the last thing you learned that made you a better developer?

choices.text: A concept I thought I understood but really didn't.
choices.response: The humbling rediscovery. Those lessons last the longest.

choices.text: A new tool that changed my workflow.
choices.response: Tool-driven growth. The right tool at the right time changes everything.

choices.text: Honestly? A mistake that cost me real time.
choices.response: Expensive education is the most permanent kind. That lesson is yours forever.

random.text: If you could remove one thing from programming, what would it be?

choices.text: Timezone handling. Please.
choices.response: THE MOST CORRECT ANSWER. Timezones are the enemy of sanity. Agreed.

choices.text: Dependency conflicts.
choices.response: The node_modules nightmare. Agreed completely.

choices.text: The expectation that we should know everything.
choices.response: Imposter syndrome culture. Yes. Knowing how to learn beats knowing everything.

random.text: What makes you feel like a real developer?

choices.text: When I solve something I didn't think I could.
choices.response: The breakthrough feeling. That's real developer confidence. It's earned.

choices.text: When someone uses something I built.
choices.response: Real users! Real impact! That's the validation that actually matters.

choices.text: Honestly, every day I'm still learning.
choices.response: Still learning is still growing. That's real. That's exactly what it feels like.

random.text: What do you do differently now compared to when you started?

choices.text: I plan before I code now.
choices.response: Thinking before typing. The discipline that makes the work better.

choices.text: I ask more questions and assume less.
choices.response: Epistemic humility! That's the hallmark of experience.

choices.text: I'm much less afraid of things I don't know.
choices.response: Fear → curiosity. That transition defines a developer's growth.
